figures.caption: Fig. 1. Qualitative examples from our collected onboard payment-action dataset, illustrating four payment modalities (Cash, QR Code, Tap, and Swipe). For each modality, we show the corresponding RGB frames and skeleton sequence extracted from the same clip, highlighting the fine-grained local hand motion patterns that motivate our multimodal design.
TABLE I SUMMARY OF THE COLLECTED TRANSIT PAYMENT-ACTION DATASET.

TABLE II (PER-CLASS) ACCURACY (%), FLOPS, AND PARAMETER COMPARISON WITH STATE-OF-THE-ART METHODS ON THE PROPOSED PAYMENT RECOGNITION DATASET. † AND †† INDICATE FUSION RESULTS WITH TWO AND FOUR ENSEMBLES, RESPECTIVELY. THE BEST AND SECOND-BEST RESULTS ARE HIGHLIGHTED IN BOLD AND UNDERLINE, RESPECTIVELY.

Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed iPay framework. The system integrates onboard surveillance RGB and skeleton streams within a multimodal mixture-ofexperts architecture consisting of an RGB expert, a skeleton expert, dual-attention fusion, and a Spatial Difference Discriminator (SDD). During training, all streams are jointly optimized with their losses summed into the final objective. During inference, the logits are aggregated to obtain the final prediction.
Fig. 3. Construction of the spatiotemporal ROI (ST-ROI). Action-relevant regions are cropped from each frame and concatenated in temporal order to form a single image for the RGB stream.

Fig. 4. Overview of the proposed Spatial Difference Discriminator (SDD), which learns adaptive spatial anchors and encodes hand-centric motion dynamics for payment behavior recognition. Orange/yellow circles: right/left hand representative joints; orange/yellow stars: adaptively learned right/left anchor points.
